records.value:
• Environmental Conservation: The learner responsibly bark-rings or girdles trees to observe translocation. (In this unit: learners analyse girdling evidence in Lesson 8 and discuss why bark must never be stripped from living trees, and how forests such as the Mau affect local water cycles.)
• Safety and Security: The learner observes safety precautions while taking nature walks and making observations on the differences between monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants. (In this unit: safe use of razor blades, iodine, eosin and nail varnish, and care when observing plants outdoors.)
• Agriculture and Food Security: The learner directly connects the mechanisms of water and nutrient transport in plants to the productivity of staple Kenyan crops (maize, beans, sukuma wiki) and to irrigation practices used by farmers in Mwea and Galana-Kulalu.
• Climate Change: The learner investigates how rising temperatures and prolonged droughts (as experienced in northern Kenya) increase transpiration rates and accelerate wilting, linking plant biology to climate adaptation strategies.
• Health Education: The learner recognises that disruption of plant nutrient transport (e.g., mineral salt deficiencies) reduces the nutritional quality of food crops such as ugali (maize flour) and sukuma wiki, with direct implications for community nutrition.

records.old: For Part C, say:
records.new: Before Part C, give a 2-minute explanation (draw it on the board) of why some plants recover and others do not. RECOVERY (temporary wilting): in the hot afternoon water loss is greater than uptake, so cells lose turgor and leaves droop; the guard cells also lose turgor, so the stomata partly close, which cuts water loss; in the cooler evening transpiration falls, the roots (still in soil that has usable water) catch up, the xylem columns are unbroken, and the cells regain turgor overnight. NO RECOVERY: when the water deficit is severe and long, the tension in the xylem becomes so large that air enters and breaks the water columns (cavitation), and root hair cells and leaf cells can be damaged by dehydration; the water highway is broken, so the plant cannot move water up even when the farmer waters again. In very dry soil below the 'permanent wilting point' the roots cannot take in water at all. Shade lowers light intensity and temperature, so transpiration and xylem tension stay lower. EXPECTED ANSWERS for the three questions: Q1 transpiration is faster than absorption and transport, so leaf cells lose turgor; Q2 as above (temporary loss and recovery versus broken columns or damaged cells); Q3 shade lowers light and temperature, so less water is lost, tension stays lower and turgor is kept. If a learner says 'the plant died because it was thirsty', ask: 'What happened to the water columns in the stem?' For Part C, say:
records.why: Why some Kibwezi plants recover by evening and others never do is part of the anchor phenomenon (and of the Final Explanation), but no lesson ever taught it: Lesson 7 promised it for Lesson 8, and Lesson 8 only mentioned it in a look-for line. A short teacher explanation and the expected answers are added to Lesson 8, and the Final Explanation hint that gave the answer away is replaced (next records). Checked against plant-physiology sources: temporary wilting reverses overnight when soil water is available; xylem cavitation (embolism) and cell damage are recognised causes of failure to recover after severe drought.
records.reference: Taiz & Zeiger, Plant Physiology (water balance of plants: wilting, permanent wilting point, cavitation); Tyree & Sperry (1989), Vulnerability of xylem to cavitation and embolism, Annual Review of Plant Physiology
records.group_headline: The anchor question 'why do some plants recover by evening while others die?' was never actually taught; Lesson 8 now explains it, gives expected answers, and the Final Explanation is aligned

records.old: (b) When transpiration is very high and the water supply is low, the tension in the xylem becomes very large. Air can enter the narrow xylem vessels and break the water column (an air embolism, or cavitation). The water highway is then broken, so water cannot reach the leaves even when the farmer waters again, and the plant dies. Plants that recover were able to keep their water columns unbroken and regain turgor in the cooler evening.
records.new: (b) Plants that recover lost more water than they took in only for a few hours: the leaves lost turgor and the stomata closed, which cut water loss; in the cooler evening transpiration fell, the roots (with water still in the soil) caught up, the xylem water columns were unbroken, and the cells regained turgor. Plants that never recover were under a much larger water deficit: when transpiration is very high and the supply is low, the tension in the xylem becomes very large. Air can enter the narrow xylem vessels and break the water column (an air embolism, or cavitation), and long dehydration can damage root hair cells and leaf cells. The water highway is then broken, so water cannot reach the leaves even when the farmer waters again, and the plant dies.
records.why: Exemplar now explains both outcomes (recovery and failure to recover) and uses the explanation taught in Lesson 8. The audit item that the lessons never taught recovery is confirmed and fixed by the Lesson 8 record.
records.reference: Taiz & Zeiger, Plant Physiology (water balance of plants); Tyree & Sperry (1989)

records.old: • The Drought-Resistant Cactus vs. the Wilting Bean: Side-by-side images of a cactus thriving in Turkana's arid landscape and a bean seedling wilting in a dry pot prompt students to ask: what structural features allow some plants to survive with almost no water? (Supports: plant adaptations — xerophytes vs. mesophytes.)
records.why: The cactus-versus-bean supporting phenomenon (xerophytes and mesophytes) is not used in any of the eight lessons, and adaptations of whole plants to dry habitats are not in the KICD content list for this sub-strand. A supporting phenomenon that is never revisited cannot support the anchor; it is removed. A teacher may instead choose to use it as an extension.

value.criterion: Scientific accuracy of the transport pathways
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly describes water and mineral entry (osmosis, active transport), upward flow in xylem and sugar flow in phloem, using the correct terms throughout.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Describes most pathways correctly with minor errors or missing terms (for example confuses one direction or omits the endodermis).
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Confuses xylem and phloem, or the processes, or gives incomplete pathways.

value.criterion: Use of evidence from the investigations
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Cites specific evidence and numbers from our lessons (potato strips, sweating leaf bag, stomatal impressions, potometer, girdled eucalyptus trees near Kericho) and links each piece to a claim.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Cites some evidence from the investigations but links it to claims only partly.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives little or no evidence, or only general statements.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Fully explains why maize wilts despite watered soil, why riverbed maize wilts sooner, why some plants recover by evening while others die, and why shaded sukuma wiki is protected, using rate of loss versus supply.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains most parts of the phenomenon but misses one (for example the shade, the riverbed or the recovery explanation).
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Explains only that the plant needs water without linking to transpiration or soil water potential.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Gives clear, logical reasoning connecting cause and effect, including cohesion-tension, the four transpiration factors, and pressure-flow.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives reasoning that is mostly logical but with gaps in one mechanism.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: States facts without explaining how or why.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Writes clearly and in order, using the key terms correctly and linking ideas to the Kibwezi farm context.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Writes understandably with a few unclear parts or terms used loosely.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Writing is hard to follow and key terms are missing or misused.

records.why: Guideline 10 asks for four CBE levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations). The data contract allows only three level fields in the rubric (excellent, proficient, developing), so a Below Expectations level cannot be represented. Suggestion: teachers add a Below Expectations column by hand when printing, or the contract is extended later.

records.old: Write your own ideas first before talking to your group.
records.new: Write your own ideas first before talking to your group — in English, Kiswahili or your home language.
records.why: No lesson gave language support for English learners. Learners may first write in the language they think in. (Kiswahili is a judgement call for the teacher.)

records.old: Say: 'Hold onto these predictions — by the end of today you will be able to check them against real biology.'
records.new: Say: 'Hold onto these predictions — by the end of today you will be able to check them against real biology.' Language support: start a word wall for the unit (xylem, phloem, transport, vascular, turgor) with simple Kiswahili links where they help — for example maji (water), mzizi (root), shina (stem), jani (leaf, plural majani), mmea (plant), kunyauka (to wilt) — and give sentence frames such as 'Xylem carries ___ from the ___ to the ___.' Teachers should confirm the Kiswahili words.
records.why: Lesson 3 introduces most of the unit's new vocabulary; a word wall, Kiswahili links for everyday words, and sentence frames help English learners. Technical terms (xylem, phloem) deliberately stay in English because KICD assessment is in English; the Kiswahili words listed are everyday words but must be confirmed by a teacher.

records.new: Allow one practice cut per group on a spare stem piece before cutting the real sample. Offer pre-cut sections to any learner with low vision, a tremor or a fear of blades, so every learner can still stain, observe and draw.
records.why: No accommodation existed for learners who cannot safely use a razor blade.

Strand and sub-strand names differ from KICD. KICD: 'Strand 2.0 Anatomy and Physiology of Plants' and 'Sub-Strand 2.2 Transport (22 lessons)'; the data uses 'Plant Anatomy and Physiology' and 'Plant Transport'. The numbers (2.0, 2.2) agree everywhere. Not renamed (the names are used in titles, file names and teacher materials); KICD also allots 22 lessons whereas this unit has 8, which is a planning matter for the teachers.
